title: Subarrays with K Different Integers
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing distinct counts versus the atMost(k) minus atMost(k minus 1) sliding window trick.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the number of contiguous subarrays that contain exactly k different integers.

blocks.caption: Exactly k distinct is computed as atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1), each a clean sliding window pass

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the number of contiguous subarrays that contain exactly k different integers.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Playlists With Exactly K Distinct Genres
blocks.text: Like scanning a long, ordered playlist for every contiguous stretch of songs that contains exactly a certain number of distinct genres, no more and no fewer.

blocks.caption: Count every contiguous subarray containing exactly k distinct values

blocks.text: Edge case: k greater than the total number of distinct values in nums
If nums never contains k distinct values in any subarray, including the entire array itself, the answer is 0.
5. How Should We Think?

Before forcing a sliding window directly onto "exactly k", notice why that direct attempt struggles: growing a window can increase the distinct count or keep it the same, and shrinking it can decrease it or keep it the same, but neither direction guarantees landing exactly on k in a way that is easy to track incrementally.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A sliding window works cleanly when a condition is monotonic, meaning growing the window never decreases the measured quantity, and shrinking it never increases it, so there is always one unambiguous direction to move to fix a violation.

Observation 2: "At most k distinct values" is exactly such a monotonic condition: growing the window can only add to or maintain the current distinct count, and shrinking it can only remove from or maintain it, giving a clean, always-correct direction to shrink whenever the count exceeds k.

Observation 3: "Exactly k distinct values" is not directly monotonic in this way, but it can be built entirely out of two "at most" computations: every subarray counted in atMost(k) either has exactly k distinct values or fewer, and every subarray counted in atMost(k-1) has strictly fewer than k.

Observation 4: Subtracting atMost(k-1) from atMost(k) removes precisely the "fewer than k" subarrays from the "at most k" count, leaving behind exactly the subarrays with precisely k distinct values, since both counts are computed over the exact same set of all subarrays.

Whenever a problem asks for an "exactly" condition that resists a direct monotonic sliding window, check whether the same condition phrased as "at most", or "at least", is monotonic, and if so, express "exactly k" as the difference of two "at most" computations.

This atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1) identity is a general-purpose trick, not specific to this problem: it converts any "exactly k" counting question into two applications of whatever monotonic sliding window already solves the "at most k" version.
6. Brute Force Solution
Check every possible subarray directly, counting how many distinct values it contains using a set, and tally those with exactly k distinct values.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every starting and ending position, extract the subarray.
Count its distinct values using a set.
If that count equals k, increment the total.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A brand new set is built for every single subarray, since the brute force makes no attempt to reuse any counting work between overlapping subarrays.

The distinct count is compared to k only after the set for that specific subarray is fully built, since a subarray's true distinct count is only known once every one of its elements has been added to the set.
The nested loop structure generates every one of the n(n+1)/2 possible contiguous subarrays exactly once, with the outer index as the start and the inner index as the end.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every subarray's true distinct count is directly computed, so every valid one is correctly counted.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) or worse, recomputing the distinct count for every subarray.
Space: O(n), for the set used per subarray.

Limitation: a direct sliding window for "exactly k distinct" is awkward, since neither growing nor shrinking the window changes the distinct count in a simple, one directional way. Recasting the problem in terms of an easier related quantity is the way forward.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's real cost comes from rebuilding a distinct-value set from scratch for every one of the n(n+1)/2 subarrays, throwing away almost all of the counting work done for the previous, heavily-overlapping subarray. A sliding window would fix that reuse problem directly, incrementally adding and removing elements instead of recounting, but only if the target condition is monotonic enough to know unambiguously which direction to shrink or grow in. "Exactly k" fails that test, but "at most k" passes it cleanly, so rather than force a window onto the harder condition, the harder condition is rebuilt out of two applications of the easier one: exactly(k) equals atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1), each of which is a single clean O(n) sliding window pass.

Counting subarrays with "at most k distinct values" is a much easier sliding window problem, since growing the window can only ever increase or keep the distinct count the same, and shrinking it can only decrease or keep it the same, a clean one directional relationship. The number of subarrays with exactly k distinct values is then simply atMost(k) minus atMost(k minus 1), since every subarray with at most k minus 1 distinct values is also counted within at most k, and subtracting removes exactly those, leaving only the ones with exactly k.
9. Optimized Solution
Implement atMost(k) using a standard sliding window, then compute the exact answer as atMost(k) minus atMost(k minus 1).
Dry run for nums = [1, 2, 1, 2, 3], k = 2 (computing atMost(2) minus atMost(1))

blocks.caption: Optimized: exactly k equals atMost(k) minus atMost(k minus 1), each computed by a sliding window

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two linear sliding window passes.
Space: O(k), for the frequency map, which never holds more than k plus 1 distinct values at once.
Why This Works

atMost(k) and atMost(k-1) are both counted over the exact same universe, every contiguous subarray of nums, so atMost(k) is precisely the set of subarrays with distinct count from 1 up to k, and atMost(k-1) is precisely those with distinct count from 1 up to k minus 1. Since the second set is entirely contained within the first, subtracting one count from the other correctly isolates only the subarrays whose distinct count is exactly k, with no overcounting or undercounting, because standard set subtraction between a set and its own subset always yields exactly the remaining elements.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Quantity","What it counts"],"rows":[["atMost(k)","Every subarray with distinct count less than or equal to k"],["atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1)","Every subarray with distinct count exactly equal to k, everything in atMost(k) except what atMost(k-1) already covers"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: atMost(k) maintains a frequency map of every value currently inside the window, using its size, the number of distinct keys, as the live distinct-value count for the current window.

The shrink loop narrows the window strictly from the left until the distinct count drops back to k or below, the one unambiguous direction that always fixes a violation of the monotonic "at most k" condition.

Adding right minus left plus 1 to the result counts every subarray ending exactly at the current right pointer and starting anywhere from left through right, since all of these subarrays share a distinct-value set that is a subset of the current window and therefore all satisfy "at most k" simultaneously.
The final answer subtracts atMost(k-1) from atMost(k) directly, needing no further per-subarray inspection once both linear passes are complete.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The "exactly k equals at most k minus at most k minus 1" reframing is a general trick whenever a direct sliding window for an exact condition is awkward, but the same condition phrased as an inequality, at most, or at least, has a clean, one directional sliding window.
Common mistakes

items: Trying to slide a window directly for the exact condition, which does not have the clean monotonic growing or shrinking property that "at most" does, leading to incorrect or overly complicated window-adjustment logic.

Forgetting to add right minus left plus 1, every subarray ending at right, starting anywhere from left onward, inside atMost, instead of just checking whether the whole current window itself satisfies the condition once.
Calling atMost with k minus 1 without a guard for k equal to 0, which would need to correctly return 0 immediately, since no subarray can ever have fewer than 0 distinct values.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: State the "exactly equals at most k minus at most k minus 1" identity explicitly and explain why atMost is the easier building block, since this reframing is the entire insight behind the problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Count subarrays or substrings with exactly some property" points toward checking whether the same property phrased as "at most" is monotonic and sliding-window-friendly, and if so, computing exactly(k) as atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1).
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you adapt this to count subarrays with at least k distinct values instead of exactly k? The total number of subarrays minus atMost(k-1) directly gives the count with at least k distinct values, reusing the same atMost building block.

Could this same "exactly equals atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1)" trick apply to other "exactly" conditions, like exactly k odd numbers in a subarray? Yes, as long as the underlying "at most k odd numbers" condition is itself monotonic under window growth and shrinkage, the identical subtraction trick applies directly.

How would you handle very large k relative to the array's total distinct value count? atMost(k) naturally saturates at counting every possible subarray once k reaches or exceeds the total number of distinct values in nums, so no special-casing is needed beyond what the sliding window already does correctly.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The canonical example of the "exactly k equals atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1)" identity, useful whenever an exact-count sliding window problem resists a direct monotonic approach.

Same underlying frequency-map sliding window technique as Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters, just paired here with the subtraction identity to handle an exact count instead of a length optimization.

Same "reframe a hard exact condition using an easier monotonic one" insight seen broadly whenever a direct approach to a problem fights against the technique being applied, rather than fitting it naturally.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) or worse time, O(n) space.
Optimized (atMost(k) minus atMost(k minus 1)): O(n) time, O(k) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: exactly(k) expressed as atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1), each computed via a monotonic sliding window
Core Idea: "Exactly k distinct" is not itself sliding-window-friendly, but "at most k distinct" is, so the exact count is recovered by subtracting two applications of the easier, monotonic condition
Time: O(n)
Space: O(k), for the frequency map used in each sliding window pass

Most Important Observation: When an "exactly" condition resists a direct sliding window, check whether the same condition as "at most" is monotonic, and express the answer as a difference of two such computations
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Exactly k equals at most k minus at most k minus 1, and at most is what actually slides
